Issued at 235 PM CDT Wed Oct 14 2026

Near zonal to southwesterly flow is found over the northern 
Plains as we remain stuck between a two upper level features. 
The first, a stacked low developing over the southern Plains, 
is expected to lift to the east this afternoon through the 
evening. With an inverted surface trough stretching to the north
and the increasing moisture returns up ahead of this low, there
are some chances (10 to 30 percent) for light precipitation 
over portions of southwestern and south central North Dakota 
late this afternoon through early this evening. Overall QPF is 
expected to be light, around a few hundreths at most for any 
given location. The second, found to the north of the forecast 
area, is a stacked low/opening trough over Alberta hat progged 
to move into Saskatchewan overnight, lofting a cold front across
the area that'll begin to turn surface winds tonight into 
Thursday morning. Otherwise, conditions today across western and
central North Dakota are expected to remain fairly calm and 
dry, with partly to mostly cloudy skies everywhere but the far 
northwest through this afternoon and seasonable highs in the mid
50s to lower 60s are expected today. With the passage of the 
cold front overnight, low temperatures across the west are 
expected to drop as low as the lower to mid 30s west to the 
upper 30s to lower 40s central. With increasing winds also 
expected behind the passage of the cold front, we will opt to 
hold back on issuing a freeze headline at this time.


For Thursday, the passage of the cold front and associated CAA 
across the area is expected to promote strong northwesterly 
winds through much of the day, with sustained speeds up to 30 
MPH and gusts up to 50 MPH expected to mix down from a fairly 
well organized low to mid level jet. The strongest winds in the 
morning and early afternoon are anticipated to be found across 
the west, and especially the southwest, as the core of the jet 
drops down across the area. Lingering strong winds are then 
expected across the south central through the evening as the 
aforementioned cold front exists to the southeast of the 
forecast area. EFI values during this period are broadly around 
0.8-0.9, with a shift of tails across portions of the northwest,
where the core of the jet is expected to linger through the 
morning and afternoon. We have opted to issue a Wind Advisory 
for all of western and central North Dakota starting 15Z 
Thursday morning through 05Z Thursday night (10 AM CDT / 9 AM 
MDT to 12 AM CDT / 11 PM MDT). Otherwise for Thursday, a few 
showers will be possible across the north central into the 
northern James River Valley in the afternoon and evening as the 
opening trough dives south across Minnesota. Seasonable cool 
highs in the mid 40s west to mid 50s south central are expected 
with the cold air mass settling over the northern Plains behind 
the front. With rapidly diminishing winds and clearing skies 
overnight, lows dropping in the mid 20s to lower 30s west can be
anticipated, which could promote a widespread freeze across 
much of the forecast area. 

Condition across the northern Plains are then expected to warm 
as we head into the end of the week as an upper level ridge 
builds in across the west, with forecast highs mainly in the 50s
on Friday becoming highs in the 60s to lower 70s for Saturday 
and Sunday. Looking ahead into next week, the ensemble has 
moderately strong agreement (approximately 85 percent of 
members) on more moderate temperatures as the ridge is squashed 
by a northern Canadian low, with highs in the 50s and 60s 
forecast through the early portions of the week. A low 
membership, underdispersed cluster (approximately 15 percent of 
members, all GEFS) also exists, which instead advertises the 
ridge surviving through the midweek, along with seasonably warm 
temperatures as high as the 60s and 70s, as the influence of the
northern Canadian low remains far to the north of the forecast 
area. Either scenario then captures a pattern shift back toward 
cooler and wetter weather in the extended turn as a strong 
Pacific low makes landfall in the southwestern CONUS and makes 
it way into the Great Plains Wednesday through the end of the 
workweek, though specifics remain uncertain this far out.
